entries.root_cause: The project-memory validator required an exact canonical visibility term that the governed human-operations document did not itself contain, so a supposedly self-consistent memory gate was born permanently failing due to vocabulary drift between authority text and validator expectations.

The new memory workflow referenced a repository-validation path that did not exist instead of reusing the already canonical validator path used by the repository, making the governance gate structurally incapable of succeeding.

The initial project-memory checkout step omitted the repository-mandated explicit unsafe-PR-checkout denial and did not bind its analysis as strongly as the established exact-head pattern, so the new governance workflow violated the repository's own workflow-safety contract.

Decision-ID uniqueness was checked across every textual reference instead of only canonical decision-definition rows, so the documented supersession mechanism would eventually be rejected by its own validator when a successor ID was both referenced and legitimately defined.

The decision register correctly separated supersession references from definition identity, but the validator did not verify that each supersession target actually resolved to one canonical defined decision, allowing broken or misspelled audit links to remain accepted.

The project-memory learning guardrail relied mainly on positive substring assertions and used an unrelated D4-C negative mutation to satisfy the strict negative-helper requirement, so the credited guardrail could stay green even if governed project-memory behavior stopped rejecting dangerous mutations.

The authoritative-visibility lesson remained protected only by a positive assertion that the current human-operations document contained the phrase. If the validator stopped enforcing that concept while the document remained unchanged, the credited guardrail would still pass and fail to detect loss of the requirement.

The project-memory ledger credited an executable falsifier stored in the D4-C assurance file, but the project-memory workflow did not invoke that falsifier and the D4-C workflow was not triggered by project-memory-only changes. A future memory regression could therefore remove the permanent rejection check without exercising it in the affected PR.

Decision supersession validation checked only that each referenced target existed, but it did not preserve source-to-target edges or reason about the resulting graph. Self-references and multi-node cycles could therefore be accepted even though no terminal current authority could be reached by following the audit chain.

Supersession extraction matched only already-valid canonical IDs. A malformed clause such as superseded by JLM-DEC-99 or JLM-DEC-O02 produced no match at all, so validation silently treated the row as current instead of rejecting a broken audit-chain declaration.

The Decision Register validator enforced only a weak minimum definition count, so deleting or corrupting one of the seeded canonical decision IDs could still leave enough rows to pass. That violated the append-or-supersede history contract by allowing accepted decision identity to disappear silently instead of remaining reconstructable.

Preserving only seeded decision IDs did not preserve their accepted meanings. A row could keep JLM-DEC-017 while reversing its proposition, silently rewriting project history without creating a successor decision or supersession edge.

Decision rows were parsed from physical Markdown lines without excluding non-rendered regions. Wrapping the canonical decision table in an HTML comment therefore preserved all IDs and meanings for the validator while removing them from the rendered project-memory document a human or recovery agent would actually read.

Workflow validation proved that mandatory run lines existed but did not prove they would execute. A required governance step could be decorated with `if: ${{ false }}` and remain textually present while GitHub Actions skipped the permanent guardrail.

The rendered-Markdown filter used lstrip while inside a fenced code block, so a fence marker indented by four or more spaces was incorrectly accepted as a closing fence even though Markdown keeps such a marker inside the code block. Hidden decision rows after the pseudo-close could therefore regain canonical authority in validation.

The workflow guard rejected only the literal plain-text spelling `if:`. YAML allows quoted mapping keys such as `"if"`, which GitHub Actions interprets as the same conditional key, so a required authority-gate step could still be skipped while textual validation remained green.

The lifecycle decision used an unescaped pipe inside an inline-code span in a Markdown table. GitHub-flavored Markdown still treats that pipe as a cell delimiter, so the rendered canonical decision record could split into the wrong columns while the validator accepted the same malformed raw representation.

The workflow validator normalized plain and quoted inline mapping keys but did not model YAML's explicit mapping-key form. A step-level `? if` followed by `: ${{ false }}` therefore remained a semantic GitHub Actions condition while bypassing the textual key recognizer.
horizontal_audit: plain quoted and explicit if spellings

entries.root_cause: Required workflow commands were validated as globally present text rather than as the executable `run` value of the uniquely named governance step. An attacker could execute `true` while moving the canonical run-shaped text under `env`, preserving the string without preserving the guardrail execution.

Rendered decision authority excluded comments and fenced code but still treated rows inside raw HTML blocks as visible Markdown. A `<script type="text/plain">` wrapper could therefore hide all seeded decisions from readers while the validator continued accepting their physical lines as canonical authority.

Exact-head checkout requirements were validated as globally present workflow text rather than as fields of the unique checkout step, and the exact commit verification command was not structurally required. A workflow could therefore check out main, move the expected ref text into an unrelated mapping, remove the verification, and still satisfy the authority validator.

Conditional-disable protection inspected only step mappings. A job-level `if: ${{ false }}` could skip the complete project-memory authority gate while every required step remained structurally present and individually valid.

Rendered Markdown authority filtering covered comments, fenced code, container tags and common block tags but omitted other GitHub-flavored Markdown raw HTML forms. Processing instructions, CDATA, declarations, and generic raw tag blocks could therefore hide all canonical decision rows while their physical text still satisfied decision validation.
